document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to your Ontario clinic with a spiral humeral fracture and several bruises of differing ages. The father's explanation of the mechanism changes during the visit and is inconsistent with the injuries. He asks you to keep everything discussed strictly between the two of you. You suspect physical abuse. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Report your suspicion to the local child welfare authority, such as the Children's Aid Society
Respect the father's request for confidentiality and arrange close clinic follow-up
Report the matter to your provincial regulatory college for direction
Obtain the father's written consent before making any external report
Wait until a repeat injury confirms the pattern before making a report

questions.explanation: Legislation defines specific instances where the public interest overrides the patient's right to confidentiality, and suspected child abuse or neglect must be reported to local child welfare authorities such as the Children's Aid Society. Physicians who fail to report in these situations are subject to prosecution and penalty and may be liable if a third party is harmed.

optionExplanations.b: Confidentiality is not absolute; statutory reporting obligations override it for suspected child abuse.
optionExplanations.c: The College is the reporting route for improper conduct of health professionals, not for suspected child abuse.
optionExplanations.d: Consent is not required for a disclosure that is mandated by law.
optionExplanations.e: The duty is triggered by suspicion, and delaying exposes the child to further harm and the physician to penalty.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with a psychotic illness tells you during a clinic visit that he intends to kill his former supervisor, whom he names and whose workplace he describes. He says he has obtained a weapon and plans to act this week. He is not currently detainable in your judgment on other grounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Notify the police and, in appropriate circumstances, warn the identified potential victim, disclosing no more information than is required to protect others
Maintain confidentiality, because Canadian courts have not expressly imposed a mandatory duty to report
Disclose his complete medical record to his former employer so the workplace can plan its response
Tell him you will disclose only if he repeats the threat at the next visit
Apply for a court order before contacting anyone outside the clinic

questions.explanation: The duty to protect applies where there is an imminent risk, to an identifiable person or group, of serious bodily harm or death. All three conditions are met here. The physician should notify the police and where appropriate the potential victim, and concerns about breaching confidentiality should not prevent this, although the disclosed information must not exceed what is required to protect others.

optionExplanations.b: Although courts have not expressly imposed a mandatory duty, physicians are permitted to warn, and the CMA Code and some regulators oblige reporting.
optionExplanations.c: Disclosure must be limited to what is required to protect others; the full record far exceeds that.
optionExplanations.d: The risk is already imminent and identifiable, so deferring action is not defensible.
optionExplanations.e: A court order is a route by which disclosure can be compelled, not a prerequisite for exercising the duty to protect.

questions.question: An Ontario patient admitted to your ward asks that a specific part of her history not be shared with any other member of the treating team, although she consents to the rest of her record being used normally. A nursing colleague who is caring for her asks you to reveal the withheld information because she is curious about it. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Respect the patient's lock box request while explaining that the law may still require or permit certain disclosures
Share the information, because express consent is not required within the circle of care
Share the information only with nurses, since they are bound by the same duty of confidentiality
Remove the information from the medical record entirely so no one can access it
Tell the patient that she cannot restrict any part of her record once she is admitted

questions.explanation: Under Ontario privacy legislation express consent is not required to share information among team members in the circle of care, but the patient may withdraw consent for that sharing and place parts of the chart in a lock box. PHIPA provisions also mean patients cannot prevent disclosures permitted or required by law, so the request is respected with that caveat.

optionExplanations.b: Implied circle of care sharing applies only until the patient withdraws consent, which she has done for this information.
optionExplanations.c: A colleague's professional obligations do not create an entitlement to information the patient has restricted, particularly out of curiosity.
optionExplanations.d: Physicians must maintain accurate and adequate records; deleting information is not an appropriate response to a lock box request.
optionExplanations.e: Patients retain the right to control their health information and may restrict specific disclosures.

source.reference: ELOM11 — Privacy of Medical Records (Lock Boxes)

questions.question: You are consenting a capable 58-year-old woman for an elective procedure. There is a small but real risk of death, and there is a reasonable non-operative alternative. She speaks limited English and her adult son offers to interpret informally. She says she simply wants to sign the form quickly. Which of the following best describes your obligation for valid informed consent?

options.text: Disclose common adverse events and all serious risks including death, describe alternatives and the consequences of declining, and make reasonable efforts to overcome the language barrier
Disclose only those risks that occur commonly, since remote risks are unlikely to affect her decision
Accept the signed form as the consent, since the signature is what documents the process
Withhold discussion of the non-operative alternative because you do not consider it clinically preferable
Ask the son to decide on her behalf, since she has delegated the discussion to him

questions.explanation: Valid consent must be voluntary, capable, specific and informed. Being informed requires the nature and expected effects of the treatment, all significant and unusual risks including common adverse events and serious risks such as death even if remote, the alternatives and their risks, and the consequences of declining. The physician is responsible for reasonable attempts to ensure understanding, including overcoming language barriers.

optionExplanations.b: Serious risks such as death must be disclosed even when remote.
optionExplanations.c: Informed consent is a process, not a transaction or a signature on a page.
optionExplanations.d: Physicians have a duty to inform patients of all legitimate therapeutic options.
optionExplanations.e: She is capable, so the decision is hers; a family member cannot substitute for a capable patient's consent.

source.reference: ELOM12 — Four Basic Requirements of Valid Consent

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a gangrenous foot refuses the amputation you have recommended, saying he would rather die than lose his leg. He explains your reasoning back to you accurately, states he understands he will likely die of sepsis, and is not delirious or delusional. His daughter demands that you proceed anyway. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Document a careful capacity assessment and respect his refusal if he is found capable
Conclude that he is incapable, because refusing life-saving surgery is not a reasonable decision
Proceed with surgery on the basis of the daughter's consent
Certify him under the Mental Health Act so that the amputation can be performed
Ask another surgeon to obtain consent, since a second opinion overrides his refusal

questions.explanation: Capable patients can refuse treatment even when refusal leads to serious harm or death, and agreement or disagreement with medical advice does not itself determine capacity. Decisions carrying a risk of serious harm do warrant careful scrutiny, so a documented capacity assessment by the treating clinician is appropriate; if he is capable, his refusal must be respected.

optionExplanations.b: Disagreement with medical advice does not establish incapacity; capacity turns on understanding and appreciation.
optionExplanations.c: A substitute decision-maker acts only for an incapable patient, and this man appears capable.
optionExplanations.d: The Mental Health Act covers detention and treatment for specific conditions and cannot be used to force unrelated surgery.
optionExplanations.e: A second opinion does not override a capable patient's refusal, and treatment without consent is battery.

questions.question: An 80-year-old Ontario woman with advanced dementia is found incapable of consenting to intubation. Her son, who is her court-appointed guardian, insists on full ventilatory support. Her daughter produces a written statement the patient made 2 years ago while capable, declining mechanical ventilation, and the son concedes he knew of it. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Challenge the guardian's decision, because a substitute decision-maker must act in accordance with wishes the patient expressed while capable
Proceed with intubation, since the guardian sits at the top of the substitute decision-maker hierarchy
Ask the daughter to consent instead, as she is relaying the patient's wishes
Follow your own assessment of the patient's best interests and withhold intubation without further process
Disregard the written statement, because wishes must be expressed verbally to be binding

questions.explanation: Substitute decision-makers must act in accordance with any wishes the person expressed when capable, and only act on best interests if those wishes are unknown. The physician may and should challenge the substitute decision-maker's final decision when the physician believes those principles are not being followed, which is the case here.

optionExplanations.b: Being highest in the hierarchy determines who decides, not that the decision may ignore prior capable wishes.
optionExplanations.c: The daughter is lower in the hierarchy; the remedy is to challenge the guardian's decision rather than substitute another relative.
optionExplanations.d: Unilateral action bypasses the required process; the physician challenges the decision rather than simply overriding it.
optionExplanations.e: Patient wishes may be expressed verbally or in written form.

questions.question: A postoperative patient receives ten times the intended dose of an anticoagulant because of a transcription error on your ward. She develops a large hematoma and requires transfusion and a prolonged admission. She is alert and asks why she is still in hospital. Your resident suggests saying only that recovery is sometimes slow. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Disclose the adverse event to the patient, express empathic regret, and report it to the appropriate health authorities
Disclose the event and tell her that the ward pharmacist was negligent
Withhold disclosure until the hospital's internal review has assigned responsibility
Avoid any apology, because an apology would be an admission of legal liability
Disclose the event to her family but not to her, to avoid causing her distress

questions.explanation: Any event that harms or threatens to harm patients must be disclosed to the patient or their decision-maker and reported to the appropriate health authorities. Physicians should offer apologies or empathic expressions of regret, which Apology Acts across Canada protect from being used as evidence of liability or negligence.

optionExplanations.b: Physicians should not suggest that an adverse event resulted from negligence, which is a legal determination, nor attribute sole responsibility to others.
optionExplanations.c: Disclosure should be prompt so the injured patient can seek corrective treatment; it does not await an internal verdict.
optionExplanations.d: Apologies are protected by Apology Acts and are not admissions of guilt or liability.
optionExplanations.e: The disclosure is owed to the patient herself, who is alert and capable.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with advanced progressive multiple sclerosis requests medical assistance in dying. She is a capable adult eligible for publicly funded health services, is in an advanced state of irreversible decline, and describes suffering that is intolerable to her. Her death is not reasonably foreseeable. Which of the following best describes a required element of her assessment process?

options.text: Her eligibility assessment must take a minimum of 90 days, unless assessments are completed sooner and she is at immediate risk of losing capacity to consent
She is ineligible, because reasonable foreseeability of natural death remains a criterion
A single assessor may provide the written confirmation that criteria are met
Ten clear days must elapse between her request and provision, with no longer period required
She may waive final consent because her condition is irreversible

questions.explanation: Under the 2021 legislative changes a patient may request MAiD even if death is not reasonably foreseeable, and in that circumstance the eligibility assessment must be a minimum of 90 days unless the assessments are completed sooner and the patient is at immediate risk of losing the capacity to consent.

optionExplanations.b: A recent update eliminated the criterion of reasonable foreseeability of natural death.
optionExplanations.c: Two independent assessors, physician or nurse practitioner, must provide written confirmation that eligibility criteria are met.
optionExplanations.d: The 10 clear day period applies to the standard pathway; her situation requires the 90 day assessment period.
optionExplanations.e: Waiver of final consent requires that death be reasonably foreseeable along with specific advance arrangements.

source.reference: ELOM20 — Medical Assistance in Dying: Bill C-14 Criteria and MAID Process

questions.question: A capable patient with metastatic cancer under your care in Ontario asks you to assess him for medical assistance in dying. You have a sincere conscientious objection to participating in MAiD and do not wish to be an assessor or provider. He becomes distressed and says he has nowhere else to turn. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Provide an effective referral to a willing and available practitioner while continuing to support him
Decline to discuss MAiD at all and continue his usual oncologic care
Tell him that no physician is compelled to participate, and leave him to find his own provider
Discharge him from your practice so that another physician takes over entirely
Agree to provide MAiD despite your objection, because patient autonomy is absolute

questions.explanation: Although nothing in Carter v. Canada compels a physician to participate in MAiD, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario mandatory referral policy, upheld by the courts, requires physicians in Ontario to provide an effective referral when they conscientiously object. Physicians must also ensure patients can access services elsewhere and are never abandoned.

optionExplanations.b: Refusing to discuss a legitimate option withholds information the patient needs and does not satisfy the referral requirement.
optionExplanations.c: It is true that participation is not compelled, but an effective referral is still required in Ontario.
optionExplanations.d: Discontinuing needed services is an act of professional misconduct unless proper alternatives and notice are arranged.
optionExplanations.e: Conscientious objection is respected; the resolution is an effective referral rather than acting against one's moral boundaries.

source.reference: ELOM21 — Physician Responsibilities Regarding Death (conscientious objection and effective referral)

questions.question: A pharmaceutical representative offers your clinic a catered lunch and learn session about a newly marketed drug, branded pens for the office, and free samples to distribute to patients. She also offers to pay your travel and registration for a conference at which you are not presenting. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline the gifts, samples and travel sponsorship, recognizing that such offers influence prescribing and that sponsorship is acceptable only when you are a presenter
Accept the pens and lunch but decline the samples and travel, since small items carry no influence
Accept the free samples so that patients can access the newest and therefore most effective drug
Accept the travel sponsorship and disclose it later, since disclosure removes the conflict of interest
Accept everything, since the pharmaceutical company shares the physician's fiduciary duty to patients

questions.explanation: Gifts or free products from industry are usually inappropriate, and the literature is clear that items such as branded pens and lunch and learn sessions influence physician decision-making. Sponsorship for travel and conference fees may be accepted only where the physician is a presenter, not merely an attendee.

optionExplanations.b: Small items such as branded pens and free lunches are exactly the offers shown to influence prescribing behaviour.
optionExplanations.c: Free samples increase patient preference for newer, costlier drugs, which are not always more effective and may have less robust safety evidence.
optionExplanations.d: Disclosure of conflicts does not eliminate the potential influence the conflict may have on physician behaviour.
optionExplanations.e: Unlike physicians, pharmaceutical and healthcare supply industries do not have a fiduciary duty to patients and are profit-driven.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man insured under his home province's health plan is visiting family in another province when he develops crushing chest pain and is taken to a local emergency department, where he is admitted with an acute coronary syndrome. His daughter asks who is responsible for paying for the emergency hospital and physician services he is receiving outside his home province. Which principle of the Canada Health Act governs this situation?

options.text: Public administration
Comprehensiveness
Universality
Portability
Accessibility

questions.explanation: Under the principle of portability, emergency health services must be available to Canadians who are outside their home province, and they are paid for by the home province. This patient is receiving emergency hospital and physician services away from home, so portability is the principle engaged. Provincial and territorial plans must comply with the five principles of the Canada Health Act to receive federal transfer payments, and the federal government can reduce its contributions to provinces that violate them.

optionExplanations.a: Public administration requires that provincial/territorial health insurance programs be administered on a not-for-profit basis by public authorities; it says nothing about care received out of province.
optionExplanations.b: Comprehensiveness requires plans to cover all medically necessary diagnostic, physician, and hospital services, but does not address where the services are delivered.
optionExplanations.c: Universality requires that all eligible residents be entitled to healthcare services; the issue here is cross-provincial payment, not entitlement.
optionExplanations.e: Accessibility requires reasonable access to medically necessary hospital and physician services without financial or other barriers within a plan's own jurisdiction.

questions.topic: Canada Health Act and Health System Organization

source.reference: ELOM3 — Principles of the Canada Health Act

questions.question: At morning rounds your team is divided over whether it is ethical to allow an inpatient to refuse a treatment the team considers life-saving. The discussion has become heated and judgmental about the patient's motives, two nurses feel their concerns have not been heard, and no one has looked at what hospital or regulatory college policy applies. What is the most appropriate next step for the most responsible physician?

options.text: Work through the case with a structured ethics framework such as IDEA, involving all relevant interprofessional colleagues, reviewing applicable hospital and college policies, and consulting a bioethicist or ethics committee
Take a vote among the team members present at rounds and proceed with the majority position
Ask the hospital's legal department to decide whether the refusal may be honoured
Defer to the opinion of the most senior physician on the team and close the discussion
Transfer the patient's care to a colleague who does not share the team's concerns

questions.explanation: Ethical issues are identifiable by the presence of a moral dilemma and are best navigated with an ethics framework; many hospitals have adopted the IDEA framework (Identify the facts, Determine the relevant ethical principles, Explore the options, Act on your decision and evaluate). The source directs the team to discuss the issue as objectively and non-judgmentally as possible, involve all relevant interprofessional colleagues, consider what hospital, university, regulatory college policies and laws apply, and consult a bioethicist and/or the appropriate ethics committees or boards. That is exactly what has not yet happened here.

optionExplanations.b: A vote does not separate facts from assumptions carrying provider bias, and it ignores the applicable policies and law the framework requires you to consider.
optionExplanations.c: Legal advice is one input, but the source frames this as an ethics process led by the team with bioethics support, not a question delegated to counsel.
optionExplanations.d: Closing the discussion silences the interprofessional colleagues the framework requires you to involve.
optionExplanations.e: Transfer is contemplated only where an option lies outside a physician's own moral boundaries, not as a way to avoid working through a team disagreement.

questions.topic: Ethics Frameworks and Managing Ethical Dilemmas

source.reference: ELOM2 — Managing Controversial and Ethical Issues in Practice (IDEA Framework)

questions.question: A 26-year-old at 30 weeks gestation with a comorbid substance use disorder declines admission to an inpatient treatment program and declines the medication you recommend. She understands and appreciates the risks to herself and to the fetus, and you judge her to have capacity. A nurse asks whether she can be kept on the ward and treated so that the fetus is protected. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Continue to offer voluntary treatment and support, and explain that she cannot be detained and treated to protect the fetus
Apply for a court order authorizing her detention and treatment in the interests of the fetus
Report the pregnancy to child welfare authorities so that the fetus can be apprehended
Tell her that the recommended treatment will be given once she loses capacity during labour
Certify her under mental health legislation on the basis of the substance use disorder alone

questions.explanation: An individual with capacity has the right to consent or refuse to consent to any medical recommendation irrespective of whether or not they are gestating, and the fetus does not have legal rights until it is born alive and with complete delivery. Winnipeg Child and Family Services (Northwest Area) v. G. (D.F.) established that a pregnant person with a comorbid substance use disorder cannot be detained and treated to protect the fetus. The correct response is to keep offering treatment while respecting reproductive autonomy, since coercing an individual into accepting medical advice is an unacceptable infringement of personal autonomy.

optionExplanations.b: The Supreme Court of Canada rejected exactly this in Winnipeg Child and Family Services; detention and treatment to protect the fetus is not available.
optionExplanations.c: The fetus has no legal rights until born alive and with complete delivery, so there is nothing for child welfare to apprehend at this stage.
optionExplanations.d: Threatening treatment at a future point of incapacity is coercive and disregards her capable refusal of the recommendation.
optionExplanations.e: Mental health certification requires that the patient meet the statutory criteria; a substance use disorder in a capable patient who is simply refusing a recommendation does not establish them.

source.reference: ELOM17 — Reproductive Technologies: Legal Issues and Arguments

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman consents to genetic testing, which confirms a pathogenic variant for a chronic condition for which surveillance is available. Her sister, who is also your patient, is likely predisposed to the same genetic condition. Your patient refuses to let you tell her sister, citing family conflict and fear of unjust social discrimination if the result is disclosed. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Maintain confidentiality, continue working with her toward consenting to disclosure, offer genetic counselling, and consult bioethics and legal counsel if complexities arise
Disclose the result to the sister at her next visit, because a duty to warn family members overrides confidentiality once a heritable risk is identified
Disclose the result to the sister, because the Genetic Non-Discrimination Act authorizes disclosure of test results to at-risk relatives
Document the refusal in the chart and raise the issue no further
Ask the laboratory to notify the sister's family physician of the result on your behalf

questions.explanation: Genetic testing requires informed consent, and consent to testing is distinct from consent to disclosure of the genetic information that results. A physician may in some specific circumstances breach confidentiality to warn family members where harm can be prevented, but in general the patient's consent is required unless the harm rises to the level of imminent risk of serious bodily harm or death — that is, an acute life-threatening condition rather than a chronic one. Because this is a chronic condition, disclosure without consent is not justified; the source recommends genetic counselling for complex information and consultation with legal counsel and bioethics if complexities arise.

optionExplanations.b: The threshold for breaching confidentiality is an imminent risk of serious bodily harm or death, not any identified heritable risk.
optionExplanations.c: The Genetic Non-Discrimination Act, in force since 2017, addresses discrimination on the basis of genetic information; it is not an authority to disclose a patient's results.
optionExplanations.d: Taking no further action abandons the ethical tension between the duty of confidentiality and the interests of at-risk family members rather than working through it.
optionExplanations.e: Routing the disclosure through the laboratory or another physician is still a disclosure without the patient's consent.

questions.topic: Genetic Testing and Disclosure to Relatives

source.reference: ELOM19 — Prenatal/Antenatal Genetic Testing: Legal Aspects

questions.question: You are the principal investigator of a clinical study that has received Research Ethics Board approval. The first eligible participant is a long-standing patient from your own clinic, who tells you she will "do whatever you think is best, doctor." Recruitment is behind schedule. What is the most appropriate way to proceed?

options.text: Arrange for a member of the research team who is not her treating physician to be the primary point of contact for recruiting and consenting her
Obtain and document her written consent yourself, after emphasizing that participation is voluntary
Enrol her now and complete the consent discussion at her next scheduled clinic visit
Ask the Research Ethics Board to waive consent for participants who are already your patients
Exclude her from the study, since a patient of an investigator may not participate in that investigator's research

questions.explanation: An ethical dilemma arises for physician researchers when their obligation to patients as their physician conflicts with their obligations and incentives as a researcher. The source states that physicians pursuing research should not be the primary point of contact responsible for recruiting and consenting their own patients, because of the possibility of therapeutic misconception and feelings of undue influence or lack of voluntariness. Her deference to your judgment is precisely the signal of undue influence that this rule is designed to address, and REB offices may themselves have requirements about who can recruit and consent.

optionExplanations.b: A verbal reassurance about voluntariness does not remove the undue influence inherent in the treating physician being the one who recruits and consents.
optionExplanations.c: REB approval and informed consent must precede participation; enrolling first and consenting later inverts the process.
optionExplanations.d: Respect for persons, expressed through informed consent, is a foundational research ethics principle; a conflict of interest is not a ground to seek its waiver.
optionExplanations.e: The safeguard is that the treating physician not be the primary recruiter and consenter, not that their patients are barred from participating.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl is brought to your emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. She is in hemorrhagic shock from a liver laceration and continues to bleed despite crystalloid resuscitation. Her parents are at the bedside, are capable, and refuse blood transfusion on religious grounds. The trauma team is ready to transfuse. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Transfuse the child, acting in her best interests given the acuity of the situation, and involve legal counsel, bioethics, and child welfare authorities as soon as possible
Respect the parents' refusal, since as the child's substitute decision-makers their decision is determinative
Withhold transfusion until an application to the Consent and Capacity Board can be heard
Withhold transfusion until a court order authorizing it has been obtained
Continue crystalloid and blood-conserving measures only, and transfer her to a centre willing to negotiate further with the parents

questions.explanation: Where substitute decision-makers make decisions that are not in the best interests of an incapable child, physicians may have grounds for administering treatment, depending on the acuity of the clinical situation. The source gives the refusal of blood transfusion on religious grounds for a child in hemorrhagic shock as the paradigm high-acuity scenario in which physicians have a stronger obligation to act in the child's best interests; in lower-acuity scenarios such as refusal of childhood immunization there is a stronger obligation to respect the decision-makers' autonomy. Consulting legal counsel, bioethics, and one's college remains advisable, but it cannot precede life-saving treatment here.

optionExplanations.b: A substitute decision-maker's authority is bounded by the child's best interests and previously expressed wishes; a decision outside those bounds may be challenged.
optionExplanations.c: Applications to a review board may be essential in less acute cases, but the child is exsanguinating and cannot wait for a hearing.
optionExplanations.d: Seeking a court order first is appropriate to lower-acuity disputes, not to a child in hemorrhagic shock with ongoing bleeding.
optionExplanations.e: Transfer delays definitive treatment and does not discharge your obligation to act in this child's best interests.

questions.topic: Refusal of Treatment on Behalf of a Child

source.reference: ELOM24 — Conscientious Objection: Patients Refusing Treatment

questions.question: A 45-year-old Métis man in your practice cannot afford the medication you have prescribed and has no private insurance. He has heard that Indigenous patients receive federal drug coverage and asks you to enrol him in the Non-Insured Health Benefits program so that his prescription and his transport to appointments are paid for. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Explain that NIHB access extends only to individuals registered under the Indian Act, individuals recognized as Inuk, and children under 18 months of a registered parent, and help him pursue provincial or territorial health insurance, social programs, or private insurance
Enrol him in NIHB, since all First Nations, Inuit, and Métis individuals in Canada are eligible for the program
Advise him to apply for registration under the Indian Act, which will make him eligible for NIHB coverage
Reassure him that once NIHB eligibility is confirmed, coverage of any medication his physician prescribes is guaranteed
Refer him to the First Nations Health Authority, which administers the NIHB program across Canada

questions.explanation: The federal Non-Insured Health Benefits program, managed by the First Nations and Inuit Health Branch of Indigenous Services Canada, relies on state-imposed definitions of Indigenous identity: access extends only to individuals registered under the Indian Act, individuals recognized as Inuk by the Inuit Land Claim Organization, and children under 18 months of age whose parent is registered First Nations or recognized Inuk. Access to care for non-status First Nations and Métis patients is consequently denied under NIHB criteria, despite similar social determinants of health and barriers to care. Clients deemed ineligible must rely on provincial or territorial health insurance, social programs, or private insurance plans.

optionExplanations.b: Métis and non-status First Nations patients are excluded by the NIHB eligibility criteria; enrolment on the basis of Indigenous identity alone is not possible.
optionExplanations.c: Indian Act registration is defined under section 6 of the Act and is not open to Métis patients simply on application; this advice sets him up for a further barrier.
optionExplanations.d: NIHB eligibility does not guarantee access to care — there are strict criteria for covered medications and procedures, and criteria change frequently.
optionExplanations.e: The First Nations Health Authority is a British Columbia body established as a step toward Indigenous self-determination in healthcare; it does not administer NIHB nationally.

source.reference: ELOM30 — Indigenous Health Coverage and Jurisdictions

questions.question: A 45-year-old male family physician in Ontario is completing the renewal of his practice licence. Over the past year he has been treated for a substance use disorder. He has been abstinent for three months, but his treating physician documents an ongoing relapse risk that may impact his ability to practice safely. He has not told anyone at his clinic. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Disclose the condition to the Medical Council of Canada
Disclose the condition to the Canadian Medical Protective Association
Disclose the condition to his provincial medical regulatory (licensing) authority, the CPSO
Disclose the condition to the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada
Disclose the condition to his provincial/territorial medical association, the Ontario Medical Association

questions.explanation: The source states that at times of license investiture and renewal, physicians must disclose if they have a condition (such as substance use disorders, or other illnesses) that may impact their ability to practice safely. That disclosure is owed to the licensing body: all practicing physicians must hold a practice license from the licensing authority in the province in which they practice, membership in it is mandatory, and its functions include maintaining ethical, legal, and competency standards, investigating complaints, and disciplining physicians. In Ontario that authority is the CPSO, and this physician is renewing his licence with a documented condition bearing on safe practice.

optionExplanations.a: The MCC is a certifying body: it certifies physicians with the LMCC, acquired by passing the MCC Qualifying Examination Parts I and II. It does not license physicians or receive fitness-to-practise disclosures.
optionExplanations.b: The CMPA is a voluntary physician-run organization providing risk management, educational programs, and legal defence against allegations of malpractice or negligence; it is not the body a licence disclosure is made to.
optionExplanations.d: The RCPSC certifies residents who complete an accredited residency program and pass the appropriate exam and monitors ongoing CME; certification is separate from provincial licensure.
optionExplanations.e: PTMAs such as the OMA are voluntary associations that negotiate fee and benefit schedules and represent physicians' economic and professional interests and offer physician health support; they hold no licensing or disciplinary mandate.

questions.question: A 57-year-old capable woman is midway through an elective procedure for which she gave written consent an hour earlier. She becomes distressed, and clearly and repeatedly tells you she wants the procedure stopped now. You judge that stopping at this point would not threaten her life or expose her to serious harm. Her signed consent form is in the chart. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the procedure now
Complete the procedure, since the signed consent form remains in effect
Complete the procedure under the emergency exception to consent
Continue while asking her substitute decision-maker to authorize completing the procedure
Continue while re-explaining the procedure and its risks, then obtain her assent

questions.explanation: The source states that consent is an ongoing process and can be withdrawn or changed after it is given, unless stopping a procedure would put the patient at risk of serious harm and the patient is not informed of or capable of considering those harms; if consent has been withdrawn during a procedure, the physician must stop treatment unless stopping the procedure would threaten the patient's life. This capable patient has withdrawn her consent and stopping threatens neither her life nor her safety, so the withdrawal must be honoured. A signed consent form is only evidence of consent and does not replace the process of obtaining valid consent, the most important component of which is what the patient understands and appreciates.

optionExplanations.b: A signed consent form is only evidence of consent; it does not replace the ongoing consent process, and consent can be withdrawn after it is given.
optionExplanations.c: The emergency exception applies where a delay would lead to serious harm or death and consent cannot be obtained from the patient or their SDM; here she is capable and stopping would not threaten her life.
optionExplanations.d: A substitute decision-maker has no role while the patient remains capable of making this decision herself; consent is sought from an SDM only for an incapable patient.
optionExplanations.e: Re-explaining the procedure and risks applies when the patient is being asked to consent to continue after a material change in circumstances (Ciarlariello v. Schachter); it does not license carrying on after consent has been withdrawn.

questions.topic: Withdrawal of Consent During a Procedure
